lines.say: Here's our goal. We want two qubits whose answers always match, even though each one alone is a fair coin flip.
Picture two dancers sharing one routine. Watch either one alone, and the moves look made up.
Watch both, and every step lines up. The routine belongs to the pair, not to either dancer.
For qubits, we use a gate called C NOT. If the control qubit is one, it flips the target.
Start with both qubits at zero, and use H to put the control in a fifty fifty superposition.
Now apply C NOT, and it acts on each part of that superposition: zero zero stays zero zero, and one zero becomes one one.
Measure the pair, and half the time you get zero zero, half the time one one.
Never zero one, never one zero. The two answers always agree.
Yet either qubit alone is a fair coin flip, and its own arrow shrinks to nothing.
That's entanglement. The pair has one shared state, and the information lives in the pair.
Here the dancers mislead us, because they follow steps written in advance.
Experiments called Bell tests show entangled qubits can't be carrying answers settled in advance.
Nor can entanglement send a message faster than light. Each side alone just sees random results.
The match only shows up when the two lists are compared.
This pair is called a Bell state, written ket zero zero plus ket one one, over root two.
So entangled qubits share one state. Each one alone is random, but together they always agree.
